title: Small Quantities: (A) Little and (A) Few
summary: Describe small amounts and small numbers using (a) little and (a) few. Understand how removing a changes the meaning from some to almost none.
learningObjectives: Choose (a) little with uncountable nouns and (a) few with plural countable nouns.
Explain the difference between a little/a few and little/few without a.
Use very little and very few to emphasise a very small amount or number.
Give short, clear answers using a little or a few when the noun is understood.

explanation.heading: Little goes with amounts; few goes with numbers
explanation.body: Use little or a little before uncountable nouns such as oil, time and flour. Use few or a few before plural countable nouns such as biscuits, tickets and days. The article a changes the meaning, not the type of noun.
explanation.example: We have a little butter and a few tomatoes.

explanation.heading: A little and a few mean some
explanation.body: A little means some, but not much. A few means some, but not many. These expressions often suggest that a small amount or number is available or useful. You can answer A little or A few without repeating a clear noun.
explanation.example: I have a few spare batteries, so you can take one.

explanation.heading: Little and few mean almost none
explanation.body: Without a, little and few emphasise a very small amount or number, almost none. They often suggest a shortage or difficulty. Little is for uncountable amounts; few is for countable plural items.
explanation.example: Few shops stay open in this village at night.

explanation.heading: Make the small quantity even smaller with very
explanation.body: Use very little for an amount and very few for a number. Keep the noun type the same: very little shade but very few trees. You can also use these expressions without a noun when the meaning is clear.
explanation.example: There is very little shade on this path.

explanation.heading: Choose a or no a for the meaning
explanation.body: A little time can mean there is some time to act; little time suggests there is almost no time. A few seats are still available, but few seats means the number is very small. Always decide whether the speaker means some or almost none.
explanation.example: The hall has few empty chairs, so we should arrive early.

comparisons.title: A small amount of something uncountable

left.label: A little = some
left.example: There is a little juice left.
left.note: A small amount remains; it is not zero.

right.label: Little = almost none
right.note: The amount remaining is extremely small.

comparisons.title: A small number of countable things

left.label: A few = some
left.example: We have a few spare chairs.
left.note: A small number of chairs are available.

right.label: Few = almost none
right.note: There are hardly any spare chairs.

examples.sentence: Could you add a little lemon juice to the salad?
examples.note: A little introduces a small amount of uncountable juice.

examples.sentence: A few boats were still on the lake at sunset.
examples.note: A few describes a small number of plural boats.

examples.sentence: We have little petrol left, so we must stop soon.
examples.note: Little suggests a serious shortage of uncountable petrol.

examples.sentence: Few customers visited the café during the storm.
examples.note: Few means the number of customers was very small.

examples.sentence: Very little light reaches this hallway.
examples.note: Very little emphasises an extremely small amount of light.

commonMistakes.incorrect: Please bring a few bread for the picnic.
commonMistakes.correct: Please bring a little bread for the picnic.
commonMistakes.why: Bread is uncountable, so use a little instead of a few.

commonMistakes.incorrect: Little tickets were left for the concert.
commonMistakes.correct: Few tickets were left for the concert.
commonMistakes.why: Tickets is plural and countable, so use few rather than little.

commonMistakes.incorrect: There are a little cups in the cupboard.
commonMistakes.correct: There are a few cups in the cupboard.
commonMistakes.why: A few modifies the plural countable noun cups.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I have very few patience with rude callers.
commonMistakes.correct: I have very little patience with rude callers.
commonMistakes.why: Patience is uncountable, so the expression is very little.

studyTips: Start with the noun: a little milk, a few oranges. Then decide whether you mean some or almost none.
Compare pairs aloud with different meanings: I have a little time / I have little time; I have a few ideas / I have few ideas.
Use very little and very few when you want to emphasise a shortage, and do not put a before these expressions.

exercises.prompt: Choose the best expression: We have ___ milk for two cups of tea—not a lot, but enough.
exercises.feedback: A little means some milk is available; milk is uncountable. Little would suggest almost none.

exercises.prompt: Choose the expression meaning almost no: ___ people were waiting at the bus stop.
exercises.feedback: Few people means almost no people. A few means some people.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct expression: There are ___ pears left, so you can take one.
exercises.feedback: Pears is plural and countable, so use a few for a small number that is available.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct word: She has ___ patience for long queues; almost none.
exercises.feedback: Patience is uncountable. Little expresses almost no patience.

exercises.prompt: We still have ___ flour—enough for one small loaf. (Use the two-word expression meaning some.)
exercises.feedback: A little is used for a small but available amount of uncountable flour.

exercises.prompt: ___ neighbours came to the meeting; almost nobody attended. (Use one word.)
exercises.feedback: Few goes with plural countable neighbours and means almost none.

exercises.prompt: Can you bring me ___ paper clips? I only need three. (Use the two-word expression.)
exercises.feedback: A few expresses a small number of countable paper clips.

exercises.prompt: There is ___ daylight left; it will be dark in a minute. (Use one word.)
exercises.feedback: Little suggests that almost no daylight remains.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: I have a few information about the bus route.
acceptedAnswers: I have a little information about the bus route.
exercises.feedback: Information is uncountable, so use a little, not a few.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: Very little guests arrived before noon.
acceptedAnswers: Very few guests arrived before noon.
exercises.feedback: Guests is plural and countable, so the correct expression is very few.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: There are a little biscuits in the tin.
acceptedAnswers: There are a few biscuits in the tin.
exercises.feedback: Biscuits is a plural countable noun, so use a few.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: We have few time to finish the game.
acceptedAnswers: We have little time to finish the game.
exercises.feedback: Time is uncountable, so little means nearly no time remains.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say the completed sentence using a little: 'There is ___ honey left in the jar.'
acceptedAnswers: There is a little honey left in the jar.
speakingExercises.feedback: Honey is uncountable; a little means some remains.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say the completed sentence using a few: 'I bought ___ postcards.'
speakingExercises.feedback: Postcards is a plural countable noun, so use a few.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say the completed sentence using very few: '___ trains stop here after midnight.'
acceptedAnswers: Very few trains stop here after midnight.
speakingExercises.feedback: Very few means that almost no trains stop here.

speakingExercises.prompt: You have some spare change, but not much. Say the complete sentence “I have ___ change.” Use a little.
speakingExercises.feedback: Change is uncountable here. A little means a small but available amount.

speakingExercises.prompt: The library has almost no computers available. Rewrite this as a complete sentence beginning “The library has” and using very few.
acceptedAnswers: The library has very few computers available.
speakingExercises.feedback: Very few with plural computers expresses an extremely small number.

speakingExercises.prompt: A friend offers you more soup. You want only a small amount. Reply with one short sentence starting “Just” and ending “please”.
speakingExercises.feedback: A little stands alone when the uncountable noun soup is already understood.

speakingExercises.prompt: Correct this sentence to mean that a small number of tickets are available: “We have a little tickets left.” Keep the words “We have” and “tickets left”.
acceptedAnswers: We have a few tickets left.
speakingExercises.feedback: A few, not a little, goes before the plural countable noun tickets.

speakingExercises.prompt: At a picnic you have a small amount of lemonade and three sandwiches. Say one complete sentence beginning “We have” and joining “a little lemonade” and “a few sandwiches” with and.
acceptedAnswers: We have a little lemonade and a few sandwiches.
speakingExercises.feedback: A little is for uncountable lemonade; a few is for plural countable sandwiches.

listeningExercises.audioText: I put a little cream in my soup.
listeningExercises.prompt: Which expression describes the amount of cream?
listeningExercises.feedback: A little means a small amount of the uncountable noun cream.

listeningExercises.audioText: Very few houses on this road have gardens.
listeningExercises.prompt: Which expression do you hear immediately before houses?
listeningExercises.feedback: Very few comes before the plural countable noun houses and means almost none.

listeningExercises.audioText: We have very little time before the shop closes.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word quantity expression you hear immediately before time.
listeningExercises.feedback: Very little emphasises an extremely small amount of time.

listeningExercises.audioText: There are a few blankets in the cupboard, so we can give one to the guest.
listeningExercises.prompt: Can the guest receive a blanket?
choices: Yes, at least one is available.
No, all the blankets are damaged.
listeningExercises.feedback: A few means a small number are available, so one can be given to the guest.

listeningExercises.audioText: There is little water in the tank, and the garden plants still need watering.
listeningExercises.prompt: What is the speaker concerned about?
choices: There may not be enough water.
The garden has too many plants to count.
listeningExercises.feedback: Little water suggests a shortage when the plants still need water.

listeningExercises.audioText: A few people came early, but very few stayed until the end.
listeningExercises.prompt: What happened by the end of the event?
choices: Only a very small number remained.
listeningExercises.feedback: Very few says that almost nobody remained until the end.

listeningExercises.audioText: Could you put a little sugar in my tea?
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word quantity expression you hear immediately before “sugar”.
listeningExercises.feedback: A little describes a small amount of the uncountable noun sugar.

listeningExercises.audioText: Very few buses run along this road on Sundays.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word quantity expression you hear immediately before “buses”.
listeningExercises.feedback: Very few goes before plural countable buses and emphasises a very small number.
